tutorials.title: Solving Equations With x in the Exponent
tutorials.body: When the unknown is stuck up in an exponent, you take the log of both sides and use the power rule to pull the exponent down where you can solve for it. The steps are: take log of both sides, move the exponent out front, then divide. This turns an impossible-looking exponential equation into a simple division. For example, to solve 2^x = 10, take logs to get x = log(10) / log(2).
tutorials.tryIt: Give me an equation like 3^x = 20 and I'll set up the log step.

tutorials.title: What a Logarithmic Scale Is
tutorials.body: On a logarithmic scale, equal steps along the axis represent multiplying by a fixed factor rather than adding a fixed amount, so each tick might mean ten times larger. This lets you display values that span a huge range, from tiny to enormous, on a single readable chart. Scientists use it for things that grow by multiplication instead of addition. For example, on a log scale the distance from 1 to 10 is the same as the distance from 10 to 100.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why earthquakes and sound are measured on log scales.

triggers: how loud is double the sound
tutorials.title: Decibels: Loudness on a Log Scale
tutorials.body: The decibel scale measures sound intensity using logarithms because our ears respond to enormous ranges of power, and logs compress that range into manageable numbers. On this scale, adding a fixed number of decibels corresponds to multiplying the sound power by a fixed factor, not just adding a little. That is why a small jump in decibels can mean a big jump in actual sound energy. For example, the difference between a whisper and a jet engine is only a few dozen decibels even though the power difference is gigantic.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why 10 dB more means ten times the sound power.

tutorials.title: The pH Scale Is Logarithmic
tutorials.body: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is using the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, which is why it runs roughly 0 to 14 instead of spanning huge raw numbers. Because it is logarithmic, each whole step on the scale means a tenfold change in acidity, not just a small change. So a drop of one pH unit means the liquid became ten times more acidic. For example, lemon juice near pH 2 is far more than twice as acidic as water near pH 7.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how much more acidic pH 4 is than pH 6.

tutorials.title: Earthquakes and the Logarithmic Richter Scale
tutorials.body: Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, so each whole-number increase in magnitude represents about ten times more ground shaking measured by a seismograph. This compresses earthquakes that range from barely detectable to catastrophic onto one tidy number line. It also explains why a seemingly small jump in magnitude is actually a massive jump in motion. For example, a magnitude 6 quake produces about ten times the amplitude of a magnitude 5 quake.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how much bigger a magnitude 7 is than a magnitude 5.

tutorials.title: Two Logs You Should Just Know
tutorials.body: Two log values come up constantly: the log of 1 in any base is always 0, and the log of the base itself is always 1. The first is true because any base raised to the power 0 equals 1, and the second because any base raised to the power 1 is just itself. Knowing these instantly speeds up a lot of log work. For example, log base 5 of 1 is 0, and log base 5 of 5 is 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Tell me a base and I'll give you its log of 1 and log of itself.

tutorials.title: Logarithmic Growth
tutorials.body: Logarithmic growth describes a quantity that rises quickly at first and then slows down more and more, the mirror image of fast-accelerating exponential growth. Its curve keeps climbing but flattens out, because reaching the next level requires a much bigger input each time. You see it whenever early progress is easy but further gains get harder. For example, the amount of practice needed to improve a skill often grows logarithmically: the first gains come fast, then later gains take far more effort.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how logarithmic growth differs from exponential growth.

tutorials.title: Adding and Subtracting Mod n
tutorials.body: To add or subtract mod n, you do the normal operation and then take the remainder mod n. The handy part is that you can reduce the inputs first or the answer at the end and get the same result. For example, mod 12, the time 9 + 7 = 16, and 16 mod 12 = 4, so 7 hours after 9 o'clock is 4 o'clock. Subtraction wraps the same way: 2 - 5 mod 12 = -3 mod 12 = 9.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (9 + 7) mod 12'.

tutorials.title: Multiplying Mod n
tutorials.body: Multiplication mod n works like ordinary multiplication, except you keep only the remainder after dividing by n. A useful shortcut is that you may reduce each factor mod n before multiplying, which keeps the numbers small. For example, mod 7, the product 4 times 5 is 20, and 20 mod 7 = 6. This is the workhorse behind hashing and cryptography, where the same operation runs on huge numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (4 × 5) mod 7'.

tutorials.title: Modular Exponentiation
tutorials.body: Modular exponentiation finds a number raised to a power, then takes the remainder mod n, without ever computing the giant power directly. The trick is to reduce mod n after each multiplication, and to square repeatedly so you reach big exponents in only a handful of steps. For example, mod 5, three squared is 9, and 9 mod 5 = 4. This is what lets RSA encryption raise numbers to enormous exponents quickly.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (3^2) mod 5'.

tutorials.title: Modular Inverse
tutorials.body: The modular inverse of a number a mod n is the number that multiplies with a to give a remainder of 1. It plays the role that dividing plays in ordinary math, since there is no direct division in modular arithmetic. An inverse exists only when a and n share no common factor other than 1. For example, mod 7, the inverse of 3 is 5, because 3 times 5 is 15, and 15 mod 7 = 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the inverse of 3 mod 7'.

tutorials.title: Congruence Mod n
tutorials.body: Two numbers are congruent mod n when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n, which is the same as saying their difference is a multiple of n. We write this with a special three-line equals sign, but the everyday meaning is that the two numbers land on the same spot when you wrap around the cycle. For instance, 17 and 5 are congruent mod 12 because both point to the 5 on a clock face. Congruence sorts every whole number into one of n groups by remainder.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'are 17 and 5 congruent mod 12'.

tutorials.title: Residue Classes
tutorials.body: A residue class mod n is the whole set of numbers that share one particular remainder when divided by n. There are exactly n of these classes, usually labeled by the remainders from 0 up to n minus 1. Mod 3, for example, every integer falls into the class of remainder 0, remainder 1, or remainder 2, so numbers like 2, 5, 8, and 11 all belong to the same class. Doing arithmetic mod n really means doing arithmetic on these classes rather than on individual numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'which residue class is 11 in mod 3'.

tutorials.title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem
tutorials.body: The Chinese Remainder Theorem says that if you know a number's remainders for several moduli that share no common factors, there is exactly one matching value within their product. It lets you stitch separate remainder clues back into a single answer. A classic riddle asks for a number leaving remainder 2 when divided by 3 and remainder 3 when divided by 5; the value 8 fits both. Computers use it to break one huge calculation into smaller independent ones run in parallel.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'find a number that is 2 mod 3 and 3 mod 5'.

tutorials.title: Euler's Theorem
tutorials.body: Euler's theorem says that if a number a shares no common factor with n, then a raised to the totient of n leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by n. The totient counts how many numbers below n are coprime to it, and this generalizes Fermat's little theorem to moduli that are not prime. For example, the totient of 10 is 4, and 3 raised to the 4th power is 81, which leaves remainder 1 mod 10. This is the property that makes RSA decryption undo encryption.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the totient of 10'.

triggers: what does phi of n mean
tutorials.title: Euler's Totient Function
tutorials.body: Euler's totient of n counts how many whole numbers from 1 up to n share no common factor with n other than 1. For a prime p the answer is simply p minus 1, because every smaller number is coprime to a prime. For 12, the coprime numbers are 1, 5, 7, and 11, so the totient of 12 is 4. This count appears anywhere you need to know how many invertible elements exist mod n.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the totient of 12'.

tutorials.title: Quadratic Residues
tutorials.body: A quadratic residue mod n is any remainder you can get by squaring a number and reducing mod n. Not every remainder is reachable this way, which is why some numbers have a square root mod n and others do not. Mod 5, squaring 1, 2, 3, and 4 gives remainders 1, 4, 4, and 1, so 1 and 4 are residues while 2 and 3 are non-residues. This split matters in cryptography and in tests for whether a number is a perfect square.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 4 a quadratic residue mod 5'.

tutorials.title: Primitive Roots
tutorials.body: A primitive root mod n is a number whose powers cycle through every nonzero remainder before repeating. It acts like a generator that can reach the whole group of invertible remainders one step at a time. Mod 7, the number 3 is a primitive root because its powers run through 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, and 1, hitting all six nonzero remainders. Primitive roots underpin Diffie-Hellman key exchange, where the cycling makes the secret hard to reverse.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 3 a primitive root mod 7'.

tutorials.title: The Discrete Logarithm
tutorials.body: The discrete logarithm asks which exponent you must raise a base to, mod n, in order to land on a given target remainder. It is the modular cousin of the ordinary logarithm, but with a wrapping number line instead of a smooth one. Mod 7, raising 3 to the power 4 gives 81, which is 4 mod 7, so the discrete log of 4 to base 3 is 4. Finding it is believed to be very hard for large n, and that difficulty is the lock behind several encryption schemes.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what power of 3 gives 4 mod 7'.

tutorials.title: Divisibility Rules and Mod
tutorials.body: The familiar divisibility shortcuts are really statements in modular arithmetic. Because 10 leaves remainder 1 mod 9, every power of 10 also leaves remainder 1, so a number and its digit sum are congruent mod 9; that is why adding the digits tests divisibility by 9. The same idea, called casting out nines, lets you spot arithmetic mistakes by checking remainders. For 1234, the digits add to 10, which is 1 mod 9, so 1234 also leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the digit sum of 1234 mod 9'.

tutorials.title: Stars and Bars
tutorials.body: Stars and bars counts how many ways to distribute identical items into distinct groups. To split n identical items among k groups, you imagine n stars in a row and slide in k-1 dividers (bars); each arrangement of stars and bars is one way. The count is the number of ways to choose where the bars go among the n + k - 1 total positions, written C(n + k - 1, k - 1). For example, handing out 7 identical candies to 3 kids (allowing zero) is C(7 + 3 - 1, 3 - 1) = C(9, 2) ways.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me how many ways to give 5 identical coins to 3 people.

tutorials.title: Circular Permutations
tutorials.body: When you arrange objects in a circle, rotations that look the same shouldn't be counted twice, so there are fewer arrangements than in a straight line. For n people around a round table, fix one person's seat as a reference and arrange the rest, giving (n - 1)! distinct arrangements instead of n!. For example, 4 friends around a table can be seated in (4 - 1)! = 3! = 6 ways. If the circle can also be flipped over (like beads on a necklace), you divide by 2 more because a mirror image counts as the same.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways 5 people can sit around a round table.

tutorials.title: Arranging Items With Repeats
tutorials.body: When some items are identical, swapping two copies doesn't make a new arrangement, so you must divide out the duplicates. To arrange n items where one value repeats a times, another b times, and so on, the count is n! divided by (a! times b! times ...). For example, the word LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice, so it has 5! / (2! times 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30 distinct arrangements. This is why a word with all different letters has more anagrams than one with repeats.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways to arrange the letters in BANANA.

tutorials.title: The Pigeonhole Principle
tutorials.body: The pigeonhole principle says that if you put more items into fewer categories than there are items, at least one category must hold two or more items. More generally, if you place n items into k boxes, some box ends up with at least the ceiling of n divided by k items. For example, in any group of 13 people at least two share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. It feels obvious, but it proves surprising facts, like the certainty that two people in a large city have the exact same number of hairs.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask why any 5 socks of 2 colors guarantee a matching pair.

triggers: how many in at least one
tutorials.title: Inclusion-Exclusion
tutorials.body: Inclusion-exclusion counts items in overlapping groups without double-counting the overlaps. For two sets you add their sizes and subtract the overlap: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|. For three sets you add the singles, subtract every pair overlap, then add back the triple overlap. For example, if 30 students take art, 25 take music, and 10 take both, the number taking at least one is 30 + 25 - 10 = 45, not 55.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many numbers from 1 to 20 are divisible by 2 or 3.

tutorials.title: Derangements
tutorials.body: A derangement is an arrangement where no item ends up in its original position. The classic story is a hat-check that returns hats randomly: how many ways can everyone get the wrong hat? The count of derangements of n items, written !n, can be found from a formula or built up step by step, and remarkably the fraction of permutations that are derangements settles near 1 over e (about 37 percent) as n grows. For example, the 3 derangements of 1,2,3 are 2-3-1, 3-1-2, and... checking each spot differs from its label gives exactly 2 valid ones for n = 3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways 4 people can all get the wrong gift.

tutorials.title: Catalan Numbers
tutorials.body: Catalan numbers count many things that involve nesting or matching without crossing, like valid arrangements of parentheses. The nth Catalan number equals C(2n, n) divided by (n + 1), giving the sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 and onward. For example, there are 5 ways to fully parenthesize a product of 4 factors, and 5 distinct shapes of a binary tree with 3 internal nodes. The same number counts paths that stay above a diagonal and ways to cut a polygon into triangles, which is why mathematicians find it everywhere.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways to match 3 pairs of parentheses correctly.

tutorials.title: The Binomial Theorem
tutorials.body: The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum, (a + b)^n, into a tidy sum of terms. Each term looks like C(n, k) times a^(n-k) times b^k, and the coefficients C(n, k) are exactly the entries in Pascal's triangle. The combinatorics reason is that expanding the product means choosing b from k of the n factors, and there are C(n, k) ways to choose them. For example, (a + b)^3 = a^3 + 3a^2 b + 3ab^2 + b^3, where 1, 3, 3, 1 is row 3 of Pascal's triangle.

tutorials.title: Pascal's Triangle
tutorials.body: Pascal's triangle is a triangle of numbers where each entry is the sum of the two numbers directly above it, with 1s down both edges. Row n (counting from 0) holds the combination values C(n, 0) through C(n, n), so the triangle is a lookup table for how many ways to choose k things from n. For example, row 4 reads 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, telling you C(4, 2) = 6 ways to choose 2 items from 4. The addition rule that builds it mirrors a real choice: an item is either in your group or not, splitting each count into the two above it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me what's in row 5 of Pascal's triangle.

tutorials.title: The Multiplication Principle
tutorials.body: The multiplication principle says that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second independent choice in n ways, the two together can be made in m times n ways, and this extends to any number of stages. It is the engine behind almost every counting formula. For example, a menu with 3 mains, 4 sides, and 2 drinks offers 3 times 4 times 2 = 24 different meals. The key condition is that each later choice has the same number of options no matter what you picked earlier.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many 4-digit PIN codes are possible.

tutorials.title: The Hockey Stick Identity
tutorials.body: The hockey stick identity says that summing a diagonal of combination values in Pascal's triangle gives the single value just below and to the side, so the sum bends like a hockey stick. In symbols, C(r, r) + C(r+1, r) + ... + C(n, r) = C(n+1, r+1). For example, C(2, 2) + C(3, 2) + C(4, 2) = 1 + 3 + 6 = 10, which equals C(5, 3) = 10. It is handy for collapsing a long sum of choose-values into one term.

tutorials.title: Arranging k Out of n (nPr)
tutorials.body: A k-permutation is an ordered selection of k items chosen from n, written P(n, k) or nPr. Because order matters and items aren't reused, you multiply the shrinking pool: n choices for the first slot, n-1 for the second, down through k factors, which equals n! divided by (n - k)!. For example, awarding gold, silver, and bronze to 8 runners gives P(8, 3) = 8 times 7 times 6 = 336 outcomes. Dividing a k-permutation count by k! removes the ordering and turns it into a combination.

tutorials.title: Counting by Bijection
tutorials.body: A bijection is a perfect one-to-one matching between two sets, and if such a matching exists the sets must have exactly the same size. Combinatorialists use this to count a hard-to-count set by pairing each of its items with an item in an easier set. For example, the number of subsets of a 3-element set equals the number of length-3 strings of yes/no, because each subset matches the string saying whether each element is included, giving 2 times 2 times 2 = 8. A related trick, double counting, finds the size of one set by counting the same collection two different ways and setting the answers equal.

tutorials.title: One-Sided Limits
tutorials.body: A one-sided limit asks what value a function approaches as you slide toward a point from only one direction: the left-hand limit comes from smaller x-values, the right-hand limit from larger ones. The two-sided limit exists only when the left and right limits agree. Think of walking toward a doorway from inside the room versus from the hallway: if you'd arrive at the same spot either way, the overall limit exists; if not, it doesn't.
tutorials.tryIt: Picture a step in a staircase: approaching the edge from the lower step and the upper step gives two different heights, so the limit there does not exist.

tutorials.title: Limit Laws
tutorials.body: Limit laws let you break a complicated limit into easier pieces: the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, the limit of a product is the product of the limits, and the limit of a constant times a function is that constant times the limit. They only apply when each individual limit actually exists. It's like splitting a grocery bill into separate items, totaling each, then adding them up rather than wrestling with the whole receipt at once.
tutorials.tryIt: If you know two functions' limits separately, multiply them to get the limit of their product.

tutorials.title: Evaluating Limits by Direct Substitution
tutorials.body: For many friendly functions, you can find a limit just by plugging the target x-value straight into the formula. This works whenever the function is continuous there, meaning it has no break, jump, or hole at that point. Polynomials always allow this, and most everyday functions do too away from trouble spots. It's like reading a thermometer right at noon because the temperature changes smoothly with no sudden jumps.
tutorials.tryIt: For a polynomial, substitute the x-value directly and that answer is the limit.

tutorials.title: Indeterminate Forms
tutorials.body: An indeterminate form shows up when direct substitution gives an expression like zero divided by zero or infinity minus infinity, which doesn't tell you the answer by itself. The form is 'indeterminate' because the true limit could turn out to be anything depending on how the pieces shrink or grow. You have to do more work, such as factoring or simplifying, to reveal it. It's like being told two runners are 'tied' without knowing whether both are sprinting or both are crawling.
tutorials.tryIt: If plugging in gives zero over zero, don't conclude the limit is one or undefined; simplify first.

triggers: how to find limits by factoring
tutorials.title: Finding Limits by Factoring
tutorials.body: When substitution gives zero over zero, try factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling a shared factor. The cancellation removes the troublesome term that was forcing the zero in the bottom, leaving a simpler expression you can then plug into. The original function had a hole at that point, but the limit still exists because the function gets arbitrarily close to that value nearby. It's like untangling a knot in a string before measuring the length you actually care about.
tutorials.tryIt: Factor top and bottom, cancel the matching factor, then substitute into what remains.

tutorials.title: Finding Limits by Rationalizing
tutorials.body: When a limit involves a square root and substitution gives zero over zero, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate, which is the same expression with the opposite sign in the middle. Multiplying by the conjugate turns the difference of roots into a difference of squares, clearing the root and exposing a factor you can cancel. After simplifying, substitute the value as usual. It's like rationalizing to clear a stubborn radical out of a fraction before you can work with it.
tutorials.tryIt: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate to clear the root, then simplify and substitute.

limit of a rational function at infinity
tutorials.title: Limits at Infinity
tutorials.body: A limit at infinity asks what value a function settles toward as x grows without bound in the positive or negative direction, describing the function's long-run end behavior. For a rational function, compare the degrees of top and bottom: the limit follows whichever part grows faster, often approaching a horizontal asymptote. A common trick is dividing every term by the highest power of x so most terms shrink toward zero. It's like asking what your average speed approaches over a road trip that never ends.

tutorials.title: Horizontal Asymptotes and Limits
tutorials.body: A horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line that a graph hugs as x heads toward positive or negative infinity, and it is defined precisely by the function's limits at infinity. If the limit as x grows large equals some fixed value, the line at that height is a horizontal asymptote. A function can approach the same asymptote on both ends or different ones on each side. Think of a cooling cup of coffee leveling off toward room temperature but never quite reaching it.
tutorials.tryIt: Take the limit as x goes to infinity; if it lands on a fixed number, that number is a horizontal asymptote.

tutorials.title: Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
tutorials.body: An infinite limit happens when a function grows without bound as x approaches a certain value, usually because the denominator shrinks toward zero while the numerator does not. We say the limit is positive or negative infinity to describe the runaway behavior, even though no actual number is reached. These points produce vertical asymptotes, where the graph shoots up or down along a vertical line. It's like the screech of feedback as a microphone gets closer and closer to its speaker.
tutorials.tryIt: If the bottom of a fraction heads to zero but the top doesn't, expect an infinite limit and a vertical asymptote.

tutorials.title: The Squeeze Theorem
tutorials.body: The squeeze theorem says that if a function is trapped between two other functions that both approach the same limit at a point, then the squeezed function must approach that limit too. It's handy when a function wiggles too wildly to evaluate directly but can be bounded above and below by tamer functions. Because the upper and lower bounds meet, there's nowhere else for the trapped function to go. It's like a younger sibling walking between two parents who arrive at the same door, so the child must arrive there as well.

tutorials.title: Continuity Defined by Limits
tutorials.body: A function is continuous at a point when three things all hold: the function is defined there, the limit exists there, and that limit equals the function's actual value. In plain terms, the curve has no hole, jump, or break at that spot, so you could trace it without lifting your pencil. If any of the three conditions fails, the function is discontinuous there. It's like a smoothly paved road versus one with a missing slab you'd have to hop over.

tutorials.title: Removable Discontinuities
tutorials.body: A removable discontinuity is a single missing point, a hole, where the limit exists but the function is either undefined there or defined to the wrong value. Because the limit exists, you could 'remove' the gap simply by redefining the function at that one point to match the limit. These often appear after a factor cancels in a fraction. It's like a knitted scarf with one dropped stitch: the pattern clearly tells you what belongs there, so the fix is a single point.

tutorials.title: The Epsilon-Delta Idea
tutorials.body: The epsilon-delta definition makes 'approaching' precise: a limit equals L if, for every tiny tolerance epsilon you demand around L, there is a small distance delta around the target x so that staying within delta keeps the output within epsilon of L. In short, no matter how strict the output target, you can always find a tight enough input window to meet it. The challenger names a tolerance and you must respond with a matching closeness. It's like promising a thermostat can hold the room within any tightness someone asks, as long as they let you set the dial close enough.

tutorials.title: Implicit Differentiation
tutorials.body: Implicit differentiation finds a derivative when y is tangled up with x and you cannot easily solve for y by itself, like a circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2. The trick is to differentiate both sides with respect to x while treating y as a hidden function of x, so every time you differentiate a y term you tack on a dy/dx by the chain rule. Then you collect all the dy/dx pieces on one side and solve for dy/dx algebraically. It is like knowing how fast a balloon's height changes even though height and width are baked into one stretched-shape equation rather than written as height equals something.

tutorials.title: Second Derivative (Concavity and Acceleration)
tutorials.body: The second derivative is just the derivative of the derivative: you differentiate once to get the rate of change, then differentiate that result again. It measures how the rate itself is changing, so a positive second derivative means the curve bends upward like a smile and a negative one means it bends downward like a frown. In a moving car, the first derivative of position is speed and the second derivative is acceleration, telling you whether your speed is rising or falling. So when your foot presses the gas harder, the second derivative is positive even before you reach top speed.

tutorials.title: Critical Points
tutorials.body: A critical point is an input where the derivative is either zero or undefined, and these are the spots where a function can switch from rising to falling or the other way around. Because the derivative is the slope, a slope of zero means the curve has momentarily flattened out, which is exactly what happens at the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley. To hunt for the highest or lowest value of a function, you first solve where the derivative equals zero to get your candidate locations. Think of tossing a ball: at the instant it reaches its peak height, its upward speed is zero, and that peak is the critical point.

tutorials.title: First Derivative Test
tutorials.body: The first derivative test decides whether a critical point is a local maximum, a local minimum, or neither by checking the sign of the derivative just before and just after that point. If the derivative is positive then negative, the function rose and then fell, so you sat at a peak; if it goes negative then positive, you bottomed out in a valley. If the sign does not flip, the point is just a flat pause, not a true high or low. It is like walking a trail: if the ground tilts up then tilts down, the spot in between was a summit.

tutorials.title: Second Derivative Test
tutorials.body: The second derivative test offers a shortcut for classifying a critical point where the first derivative is zero: just plug that point into the second derivative. If the second derivative is positive the curve is bending upward like a bowl, so you have a local minimum, and if it is negative the curve bends downward like a dome, giving a local maximum. When the second derivative is zero the test is inconclusive and you fall back on the first derivative test. Picture a marble: it settles in a bowl-shaped dip (positive concavity, a minimum) but rolls off a dome-shaped bump (negative concavity, a maximum).

tutorials.title: Inflection Points
tutorials.body: An inflection point is where a curve changes its concavity, switching from bending upward to bending downward or the reverse, which shows up as the second derivative changing sign. It is not about the curve being highest or lowest, but about the moment its bend reverses direction. You find candidates by setting the second derivative to zero and then confirming the sign actually flips on either side. Think of an S-shaped slide: there is a point in the middle where it stops curving one way and starts curving the other, and that turning of the bend is the inflection point.

tutorials.title: Related Rates
tutorials.body: Related rates problems link two or more quantities through an equation and ask how fast one changes given how fast another changes. You differentiate the connecting equation with respect to time, which pulls in a rate (a per-second term) for every changing variable, then plug in the known rate to solve for the unknown one. The key insight is that the chain rule ties each variable's change to the clock. A classic example is a ladder sliding down a wall: because the ladder length is fixed, knowing how fast the foot slides outward lets you compute how fast the top slides down.

tutorials.title: Partial Derivatives
tutorials.body: A partial derivative measures how a function of several variables changes when you nudge just one input while holding all the others frozen. You differentiate normally with respect to the chosen variable and treat every other variable as if it were a fixed constant. This lets you isolate the influence of a single ingredient in a recipe with many. Imagine the temperature in a room depending on both your distance from the heater and the time of day: the partial derivative with respect to distance tells you how temperature changes as you step closer, pretending the clock has stopped.
